{{Short description|Banach space with a compatible structure of a lattice}}
In the [[mathematics|mathematical disciplines]] of in [[functional analysis]] and [[order theory]], a '''Banach lattice''' {{math|(''X'',‖·‖)}} is a [[Banach space|complete normed vector space]] with a [[lattice order]], <math>\leq</math>, such that for all {{math|''x'', ''y'' ∈ ''X''}}, the implication <math display=block>{|x|\leq|y|}\Rightarrow{\|x\|\leq\|y\|}</math> holds, where the absolute value {{math|{{pipe}}·{{pipe}}}} is defined as <math display=block>|x| = x \vee -x := \sup\{x, -x\}\text{.}</math>  

== Examples and constructions ==
Banach lattices are extremely common in functional analysis, and "every known example [in 1948] of a Banach space [was] also a [[vector lattice]]."{{sfn|Birkhoff|1948|p=246}}  In particular:
* {{math|{{mathbb|R}}}}, together with its absolute value as a norm, is a Banach lattice.
* Let {{mvar|X}} be a topological space, {{mvar|Y}} a Banach lattice and {{math|𝒞(''X'',''Y'')}} the [[space of continuous bounded functions]] from {{mvar|X}} to {{mvar|Y}} with norm <math display=block>\|f\|_{\infty} = \sup_{x \in X} \|f(x)\|_Y\text{.}</math> Then {{math|𝒞(''X'',''Y'')}} is a Banach lattice under the pointwise partial order: <math display=block>{f \leq g}\Leftrightarrow(\forall x\in X)(f(x)\leq g(x))\text{.}</math>  

Examples of non-lattice Banach spaces are now known; [[James space|James' space]] is one such.<ref>Kania, Tomasz (12 April 2017).  [https://math.stackexchange.com/a/2230649 Answer] to "Banach space that is not a Banach lattice" (accessed 13 August 2022).  ''Mathematics StackExchange''.  [[Stack Exchange|StackOverflow]].</ref>  

== Properties ==
The continuous dual space of a Banach lattice is equal to its [[Order dual (functional analysis)|order dual]].{{sfn|Schaefer|Wolff|1999|pp=234–242}} 

Every Banach lattice admits a [[approximate identity|continuous approximation to the identity]].{{sfn|Birkhoff|1948|p=251}}

==Abstract (L)-spaces==
A Banach lattice satisfying the additional condition <math display=block>{f,g\geq0}\Rightarrow\|f+g\|=\|f\|+\|g\|</math> is called an abstract (L)-space.  Such spaces, under the assumption of separability, are isomorphic to closed sublattices of {{math|''L''<sup>1</sup>({{closed-closed|0,1}})}}.{{sfn|Birkhoff|1948|pp=250,254}}  The classical [[mean ergodic theorem]] and [[Poincaré recurrence]] generalize to abstract (L)-spaces.{{sfn|Birkhoff|1948|pp=269-271}}
